youtube.baslik: Inner Ear Malformations: The Sennaroglu Classification | Lesson 238 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How are inner ear malformations classified, and how do they affect the implant decision? In this lesson we learn the eight groups of the Sennaroglu classification: Michel aplasia, cochlear aplasia, common cavity and cochlear hypoplasia, incomplete partition types 1, 2 and 3, cochlear aperture abnormalities, and the choice between a cochlear implant and an auditory brainstem implant.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Sennaroğlu and Saatçi (2002), A new classification for cochleovestibular malformations, The Laryngoscope; Sennaroğlu and Bajin (2017), Classification and Current Management of Inner Ear Malformations, Balkan Medical Journal; Jackler, Luxford and House (1987), Congenital malformations of the inner ear: a classification based on embryogenesis, The Laryngoscope; Social Security Institution, Health Implementation Communiqué (SUT), Türkiye, section 3.3.33 Auditory implants.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: The Sennaroglu classification and the implant decision
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.

cumleler.yazi: In this lesson we will learn about inner ear malformations and the Sennaroglu classification, the most widely used system today.
cumleler.ses: In this lesson we will learn about inner ear malformations and the Sennarolu classification, the most widely used system today.

cumleler: We will look at how each group affects hearing and the choice between a cochlear implant and an auditory brainstem implant.

maddeler.metin: About one fifth of congenital losses
Seen on imaging: CT and MRI

yan.metin: Inner ear malformation *visible on imaging* in congenital loss

cumleler: In about 20 percent of congenital sensorineural hearing losses, imaging shows a detectable inner ear malformation.
In most of the rest, the problem lies in the membranous labyrinth and is not visible on computed tomography, or CT, or on MRI.
Visible malformations reflect arrested development of the cochlea, vestibule, canals and internal auditory canal.
The type of malformation determines whether a cochlear implant is possible or an auditory brainstem implant is needed.
It also affects surgical risks, electrode choice, programming and the expectations shared with the family.
So a common language, that is, a reliable classification, is needed by every member of the implant team.
Incomplete development of the cochlea was first described in the eighteenth century by the Italian physician Mondini.

cumleler.yazi: In 1987, Jackler and colleagues proposed a classification that ordered malformations by the week in which development stopped.
cumleler.ses: In nineteen eighty seven, Jackler and colleagues proposed a classification that ordered malformations by the week in which development stopped.

cumleler.yazi: In 2002, Sennaroglu and Saatci of Hacettepe University published a new classification and defined incomplete partition types 1 and 2.
cumleler.ses: In two thousand two, Sennarolu and Saatchi of Hacettepe University published a new classification and defined incomplete partition types one and two.

cumleler: Type 3 was added later, and the classification has been updated over the years.

cumleler.yazi: The 2017 review by Sennaroglu and Bajin groups malformations into eight main groups; this is the most widely used system today.
cumleler.ses: The twenty seventeen review by Sennarolu and Bajin groups malformations into eight main groups; this is the most widely used system today.

cumleler: The first group is complete labyrinthine aplasia, where the inner ear never developed, that is, Michel aplasia.
The second is the rudimentary otocyst; only a millimetric remnant of the inner ear is present.
The third is cochlear aplasia; the cochlea is absent, while the vestibule and canals may be present.
The fourth is the common cavity; the cochlea and vestibule have not separated and form a single cavity.
The fifth is cochlear hypoplasia; the cochlea is separated but smaller than normal.
The sixth is incomplete partition; the outer size of the cochlea is near normal, but its inner partitions are missing.
The last two groups are enlarged vestibular aqueduct and abnormalities of the cochlear aperture, through which the cochlear nerve passes.
The groups run roughly from the malformation in which development stopped earliest, around the third week, to later stages.
In Michel aplasia, the cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals and aqueducts have not developed.
These children either have no auditory response at all or only low-frequency responses that may come from vibrotactile sensation.
In a rudimentary otocyst, a small remnant of the inner ear exists, but there is no internal auditory canal or connection to the brainstem.
In cochlear aplasia, the cochlea is absent; the vestibule may be normal or enlarged.
In these three groups, there is no cochlea in which to place an electrode, so a cochlear implant is not possible.
The option is an auditory brainstem implant, whose electrodes are placed directly on the cochlear nucleus in the brainstem.
The drawing on screen shows a normal labyrinth; in these malformations, the highlighted cochlear part never developed.

notlar.metin: If a nerve exists: special electrode

cumleler: In a common cavity, the cochlea and vestibule form a single round or oval cavity.
The internal auditory canal opens into the middle of this cavity, and the nerve is an undivided common cochleovestibular nerve.
If a nerve is present, a cochlear implant can be placed; special straight electrodes are used so the electrode sits against the cavity wall.
Because no tonotopic order is expected, outcomes are more variable than with a normal cochlea.
If there is no nerve, or progress with the implant is poor, an auditory brainstem implant is considered.
A common cavity must be told apart from cochlear aplasia with an enlarged vestibule, because no cochlear implant is placed in the latter.
In cochlear hypoplasia type 1, the cochlea is like a small bud with no inner structure.
In type 2, the outline is preserved, but the cochlea looks cystic and the modiolus is defective; cerebrospinal fluid may leak.
In type 3, the cochlea has fewer than two turns and the modiolus is short.
In type 4, the basal turn is normal; the middle and apical turns are small and displaced anteriorly.
In this group, hearing can range from normal to profound loss; a conductive component from stapes fixation can also be seen.
For mild and moderate losses, hearing aids are considered; for severe losses with a nerve present, an implant with thin, short electrodes.
If the cochlear nerve is absent, an auditory brainstem implant is the option.
In incomplete partition type 1, the cochlea looks cystic; the modiolus and septa are absent, and the vestibule is enlarged.
In this type, a cerebrospinal fluid gusher in surgery is common, with a risk of recurrent meningitis through a defective footplate.
In type 2, the basal turn is normal; the middle and apical turns merge into a cystic apex, and the apical part of the modiolus is missing.
Type 2 comes with a mildly enlarged vestibule and an enlarged vestibular aqueduct; this triad is called the Mondini deformity.
In type 3, the septa are present, but the modiolus is completely absent and the cochlea opens directly into the internal auditory canal.
Type 3 is linked to X-linked hearing loss and is usually seen in males.
Hearing is usually severe to profound in type 1, variable and progressive in type 2, and often mixed in type 3.
Type 2 is the best-known malformation; together with the vestibular and aqueduct findings, it is called the Mondini deformity.
The basal turn at the base of the cochlea, and the nerve fibers there, are largely normal.
Because this region, which carries the high frequencies, is preserved, implant outcomes are usually good.
At the apex, however, the middle and apical turns have not separated and form a cystic space.
Hearing can fluctuate and drop suddenly after head trauma; we saw this in the lesson on enlarged vestibular aqueduct.
Hearing aids are used first; when the loss progresses and aids are no longer enough, a cochlear implant is placed.
In type 3, because there is no modiolus, there is no bony boundary between the cochlea and the internal auditory canal.
So the loss is often mixed, and the conductive component can resemble otosclerosis.
If stapes surgery is done on this ear, perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid can gush out; the classification advises avoiding stapes surgery.
During cochlear implant surgery, a fluid gusher is expected, and the electrode can accidentally advance into the internal auditory canal.
That is why confirming the electrode position with imaging during surgery is recommended.

cumleler.yazi: Type 3 is linked to variants of the POU3F4 gene on the X chromosome; genetic counseling is important for the family.
cumleler.ses: Type three is linked to variants of the P O U three F four gene on the X chromosome; genetic counseling is important for the family.

maddeler.metin: Bony canal of the cochlear nerve
Internal auditory canal may be narrow

cumleler: The cochlear aperture is the bony canal through which the cochlear nerve passes from the internal auditory canal into the cochlea.

cumleler.yazi: Sennaroglu and Bajin define a canal narrower than 1.4 millimeters as hypoplasia, and its absence as aplasia.
cumleler.ses: Sennarolu and Bajin define a canal narrower than one point four millimeters as hypoplasia, and its absence as aplasia.

cumleler: These conditions often come with a narrow internal auditory canal and an underdeveloped or absent cochlear nerve.
Because hair cells may be intact, otoacoustic emissions, or OAEs, may be present; a child can pass an OAE-only screening.
In these children, hearing aids usually fall short; if the nerve is underdeveloped, an implant may be considered after a hearing aid trial.
If the canal and nerve are completely absent, the first option is an auditory brainstem implant.

cumleler.yazi: The seventh group is enlarged vestibular aqueduct; the criterion is an aqueduct wider than 1.5 millimeters at its midpoint.
cumleler.ses: The seventh group is enlarged vestibular aqueduct; the criterion is an aqueduct wider than one and a half millimeters at its midpoint.

cumleler: In this group, the cochlea, vestibule and canals are normal; hearing often fluctuates and progresses.
Because hearing can drop suddenly after head trauma, the family is informed.
When the loss reaches a profound level, a cochlear implant is a good option; we saw this earlier in a separate lesson.
In terms of clinical management, this group is approached much like incomplete partition type 2.
The first question on the decision path is whether there is a cochlea in which an electrode can be placed.
The second question is whether there is a cochlear nerve to stimulate; MRI shows this best.
If the cochlea and nerve are present, a cochlear implant is placed with an electrode suited to the malformation.
If the cochlea or cochlear nerve is absent, the option is an auditory brainstem implant; in Türkiye, the SUT also covers this implant.
In uncertain cases where the nerve is very thin, some centers try an implant first and track progress.
In selected cases, combining the two methods may also be considered.
In every case, the decision is made by the team, based on audiological findings, imaging and discussion with the family.
In some malformations, perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid can gush out during surgery; the surgeon prepares for this in advance.
In some types, such as incomplete partition type 1, meningitis risk is higher; vaccination and informing the family are important.
The course of the facial nerve can vary, which matters both for surgery and for unwanted facial nerve stimulation by the implant.
Electrode length and shape are chosen according to the type of malformation.
Programming may need higher stimulation levels and some electrodes may be turned off; the audiologist works with the imaging report in mind.
The family is given a realistic picture of expectations specific to the type of malformation.

sahneler.metin: In a child with a conductive component, especially a boy with a family history, raise in your report whether imaging is needed to rule out an inner ear malformation.
cumleler: A tip from the field: in a child with mixed or conductive loss, not every air-bone gap is a middle ear problem.
Incomplete partition type 3 and enlarged vestibular aqueduct can also create a conductive component.
Especially in a boy, and when the family has similar hearing loss, bring this possibility to the physician's attention in your report.
This finding is a reminder of the importance of imaging before any middle ear surgery is considered.

maddeler.metin: Eight groups, by time of arrest
Nerve and aperture: implant or brainstem

cumleler.yazi: The Sennaroglu classification groups inner ear malformations into eight main groups by the stage at which development stopped.
cumleler.ses: The Sennarolu classification groups inner ear malformations into eight main groups by the stage at which development stopped.

cumleler: In Michel aplasia, rudimentary otocyst and cochlear aplasia, there is no cochlea, so the option is an auditory brainstem implant.
The three types of incomplete partition carry different surgical risks; type 2 usually does well, and type 3 avoids stapes surgery.
The status of the cochlear aperture and cochlear nerve decides between a cochlear implant and a brainstem implant.

sahneler.soru: In which malformation is a cochlear implant not possible?
sahneler.aciklama: In Michel aplasia there is no inner ear; the option is a _brainstem implant_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in which of these malformations is a cochlear implant not possible?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: Michel aplasia.
In this malformation, the inner ear never developed; with no cochlea for an electrode, the option is an auditory brainstem implant.
